title: Obesity is a disease: Why is insurance still a barrier to treatment?

contentHtml:
Dr Aparna Govil Bhasker, Consultant Bariatric and Laparoscopic Surgeon, MetaHeal Clinic, Mumbai, highlights the challenges patients face in securing insurance coverage for bariatric surgery, the gaps between policy provisions and their implementation, and the need for a more transparent and time-bound claims process to ensure timely access to medically necessary treatment

For many people living with severe obesity, deciding to undergo bariatric surgery is often the hardest step in their treatment journey.

Most have struggled with their weight for years, trying diets, exercise, medications and lifestyle changes. Surgery brings understandable fears, and patients must often overcome family resistance and the persistent stigma that bariatric surgery is an “easy way out”. Reaching the point where a patient finally says, “I am ready for surgery,” may itself take months or years.

Having finally overcome fear and stigma to choose surgery, patients should be able to move towards treatment. Instead, many find themselves entering an exhausting battle for insurance approval.

IRDAI criteria are relatively clear. Surgery should be advised by a doctor, supported by clinical protocols, and the patient should be over 18 years, with a BMI ≥40 kg/m², or ≥35 kg/m² with specified severe comorbidities after failure of less invasive weight-loss methods. These include severe sleep apnoea, uncontrolled type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease and obesity-related cardiomyopathy.

Yet there is a troubling disconnect between policy and implementation.

Patients may face repeated queries about the “cause” and duration of their obesity, demands for old records and repeated evidence of previous weight-loss attempts. Even patients who clearly fulfil eligibility criteria may be subjected to “deep verification”, home visits or requests for geotagged photographs. Sometimes, repeated communication is followed by prolonged silence or denial without a clearly understandable medical reason.

Insurers have every right to verify claims and prevent fraud. But verification must be proportionate, relevant and time-bound. Due diligence should not become an endurance test for a patient seeking treatment.

It also risks perpetuating obesity stigma. If obesity is a chronic disease, why must patients repeatedly prove that they have “tried hard enough” or that their disease genuinely deserves treatment?

These experiences are not isolated. In our OSSI survey of 109 bariatric surgeons, nearly 70% described insurance approval as complex or very complex, over 91% found it more cumbersome than approval for routine surgeries, and 95.4% reported that eligible patients delay surgery while awaiting insurance approval.

And delay is not benign.

Severe obesity is progressive. Diabetes and sleep apnoea can worsen, mobility can decline, and cardiovascular risk accumulates. Over time, obesity and its metabolic consequences contribute to coronary disease, heart failure, stroke and significant morbidity.

There is a disturbing paradox here: must a patient become sicker before treatment becomes easier to justify? Indeed, coronary heart disease and obesity-related cardiomyopathy are themselves among the comorbidities recognised within the insurance criteria.

Treatment delayed can become treatment denied.

The answer is not less scrutiny, but better scrutiny — standardised documentation, medically relevant queries, defined timelines, transparent reasons for denial and meaningful specialist review when required.

Perhaps we also need a change in approach. Once a genuine claim fulfils clearly defined medical criteria, the process should move from repeatedly searching for additional hurdles to facilitating appropriate treatment while maintaining necessary safeguards.

Most importantly, we must remember the person at the centre of all this. A patient who has overcome fear and stigma, accepted the need for surgery and fulfilled the prescribed criteria should not then have to fight an exhausting administrative battle to access treatment.

We have recognised obesity as a disease. Our policies have begun to reflect that recognition. It is time our processes did too. Insurance should be a bridge to medically necessary care — not another barrier standing in its way.
